data.title: Chinese Firms Going Global Must Invest in Trust and Time, Experts Say
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 23 -- Chinese companies expanding overseas need to build trust with local stakeholders and commit to long-term investment rather than relying solely on sales, experts said during a roundtable discussion at an event marking the 10th anniversary of Yicai Global, the English-language news service of Yicai Media Group.

Compared with multinationals that possess nearly a century of international experience, Chinese firms' global journey is just getting started, so there is a lot they can learn, Chen Juan, editor-in-chief of Yicai Global, said at the event held in Shanghai on Oct. 21. This year, Yicai Global reporters followed Chinese supply chains south to semiconductor plants in Penang, nickel projects in Indonesia, and infrastructure sites in Dhaka for the news outlet's series The Southern Journey, she pointed out.

"Older multinationals have paid tuition for decades, and we don't need to pay it all over again," Chen stressed.

Trust Before Exposure

The environment Chinese firms face abroad is fundamentally different from the one foreign companies found when they came to China, said Jiang Yan, founding partner of Nexa Consulting and a veteran international communications specialist. "When foreign companies entered the Chinese market, the timing was very favorable, and the market welcomed them."

However, Chinese brand exports and overall China's product exports face a trust problem, she noted.

Chinese companies face what Jiang called "preemptive identity skepticism" in the current geopolitical climate, making it hard for them to find strong third-party endorsements in host countries. They need to pick topics and communicate via messages different target audiences can understand and resonate, because governments care more about compliance and tax, business partners about joint research and development, local supply chains, and long-term commitment, and consumers about user experience, she pointed out.

Firms should also prepare a reactive plan alongside a proactive one, especially at high-profile moments such as listing overseas, because dodging tough questions makes them look as if they have something to hide, Jiang stressed. "AI is very convenient now. If you don't speak, your competitors will speak for you, and they will define you."

Local partners routinely ask search engines and artificial intelligence chatbots whether a Chinese company is reliable, said Chris Pereira, founder and chief executive of iMpact, which has supported more than 500 Chinese companies in localizing. "AI will give an answer, and that answer will decide whether overseas resources work with the company or not," he noted, adding that such tools draw only on authoritative, credible sources rather than companies' own promotion.

In addition, Pereira rejected the idea that globalization is in retreat, calling that an American view. The overseas expansion of Chinese firms is a feature of a "new generation of globalization," he stressed.

People and Compliance

Chinese firms should distinguish between internationalization and globalization, noted Michael Chen, founder and CEO of human resources and payroll technology provider BIPO, which serves clients in more than 170 markets. Internationalization often means a company going abroad to expand its business, while globalization is seeing every region as part of one market, he pointed out.

"When we look with a more global perspective, we can absorb the good things from every country and every region with a humbler and more inclusive mindset," Chen added.

Chen, who has worked at multinationals such as logistics giant DHL Group in legal and HR roles, said Chinese firms are still building three capabilities that older multinationals have long had: a pool of international talent, a complete global authorization system, and the mechanisms to delegate authority while staying in control.

Work culture is another hurdle, according to Chen. "To keep overseas operations in step with the demands of the boss and management, HR teams often want to hire people abroad who are hyper-competitive, but in fact that is very hard to come by in Europe, the US and Singapore. If you push them to a certain point, they may just quit.'"

Data privacy is the compliance risk Chinese firms should take most seriously overseas, Chen stressed. A wrongful dismissal leads to a simple compensation, but a breach of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation can bring fines of up to EUR20 million (USD22.5 million) or 4 percent of the previous year's global turnover, whichever is higher, he noted. "Doing well on efficiency gives us an edge in competition, but doing well on compliance lets us go further."

The Value of Time

Lu Yao, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of Journalism, pointed to multinationals' scholarship programs as an example of patient investment.

Chinese firms' overseas investments tend to be project-based and short-term, Lu pointed out, advising them to start small, think long-term, and govern jointly, adding that local partners should be ones they can work with for 20 years or more, with several companies able to jointly fund a program.

However, firms should not expect scholarships to vouch for them, since reputations ultimately depend on operating lawfully and honestly in the host country, Lu said. "The shortest investment is ad placement, and the longest is a person who carries an experience and lives in one place for decades."

All panelists at the roundtable pointed to the same question, Chen Juan said in her closing: "How can Chinese companies become part of local societies, rather than just outside businessmen?"

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: China’s Geely, Nio Strengthen Battery-Swap Alliance With Cross-Shareholding Deal
data.description:
(Yicai) Sept. 28 -- Chinese automotive giant Geely Holding Group and electric vehicle manufacturer Nio will deepen their strategic cooperation on battery swapping and EV charging through a cross-shareholding arrangement at the subsidiary level, aimed at accelerating the expansion of their battery-swap and charging service networks.

Geely will use its 100 percent equity in its battery-swap service provider Yiyi Internet Technology and CNY640 million (USD95.3 million) in cash to subscribe to newly issued shares in Nio’s battery-swap and charging unit Nio Power, Shanghai-based Nio said today. Upon completion of the transaction, Geely will hold a 30 percent stake in Nio Power, which will have a post-investment valuation of CNY16 billion (USD2.4 billion).

Nio was one of the earliest Chinese EV manufacturers to adopt battery swapping and set up Nio Power in 2017 to develop and run a battery-swap and charging service network. As of Sept. 20, Nio operated 4,099 battery-swap stations and 5,289 charging stations, and had provided users with over 120 million battery swaps in total, it said.

Yiyi, founded in 2017, managed more than 470 battery-swap stations in over 40 cities across China as of April last year, and has plans to expand to 2,000 stations by next year, according to its website.

The integration of Yiyi into Nio Power will accelerate the expansion of Nio's battery swapping network, with the aim of building 10,000 battery-swap stations by 2030, Nio said. The two sides will also work together to establish unified battery-swapping technology standards, while Hangzhou-based Geely will develop battery-swap vehicles models for consumers.

Nio will also acquire a stake in Geely’s EV charging service provider Zhejiang Haohan Energy Technology, according to the agreement between the two parties. Upon completion of the transaction, Nio will hold a 10 percent stake in Haohan, and both sides will share resources to expand charging network coverage and improve operational efficiency.

Haohan currently operates 2,500 charging stations and 12,000 charging guns in 232 cities across China. By the end of 2027, it plans to expand its network to 22,000 charging stations and 100,000 charging guns, Geely said.

The collaboration between Nio and Geely dates back to November 2023, when Nio announced plans to form a battery swapping alliance with automakers. Since then, it has established partnerships with eight automakers, including Changan Automobile and Geely.

Editor: Kim Taylor

data.title: AI Cuts Costs in USD6 Billion Overseas Short Drama Market, But Can It Win Viewers?
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 23 -- Artificial intelligence is accelerating the overseas expansion of Chinese short dramas, driving growth in a market forecast to exceed USD6 billion this year, even as audience acceptance remains a hurdle.

The overseas micro-short drama market is expected to exceed USD6 billion this year, up about 50 percent from 2025, according to DataEye Research Institute. The research body focusing on digital entertainment raised its forecast by USD1 billion from the beginning of the year as AI-generated dramas and animated short dramas expanded content supply.

Micro-dramas, a format popularized in China, typically feature episodes lasting just a few minutes, with cliffhangers designed to keep smartphone viewers watching and paying to unlock more episodes. As the format expands overseas, TikTok and YouTube are stepping up content partnerships, further driving industry growth, DataEye said. But the rapid expansion of AI-generated content is also testing overseas audiences' appetite for the format.

AI Reshapes Overseas Competition

AI is helping established players expand while giving newer competitors room to grow.

He Yunchang, founder of micro-drama producer Maiya Media, told Yicai at a YouTube forum yesterday that AI had helped the company rise from the second tier to the top tier of the overseas market over the past two years. “In 2026, we mainly seized the opportunities brought by AI.”

Maiya Media began expanding into overseas short drama distribution in September 2024. Despite entering the market later than many competitors, its short drama platform called NetShort has attracted about 80 million monthly active users in roughly two years, according to He.

Based on numbers from DataEye, NetShort ranked second among overseas short drama apps by combined in-app purchase revenue on the two major mobile operating systems in September.

AI is helping foreign markets narrow the gap with China's more mature industry for bite-sized entertainment. The overseas short drama market previously lagged behind China's in development, but AI has become an important driver of growth this year, Nan Yapeng, vice president of Crazy Maple Studio, told Yicai. Crazy Maple runs micro-drama platform ReelShort.

Several AI-generated short dramas released on ReelShort since the second quarter have performed well, Nan said. Advances in large language models have improved production efficiency while broadening the range of themes and genres that creators can explore.

The technology also enables producers to explore content that would be difficult to bring to life through live-action filming, Nan added.

He from Maiya Media said that AI has also improved the baseline quality of scripts. While scripts written without AI assistance previously scored between 50 and 85 points, AI-assisted drafts can score at least 75, the founder of Maiya Media said, without specifying how they were evaluated. Senior editors can then further improve the drafts, he added.

Beyond helping leading platforms produce more content, AI is also lowering barriers to entry, allowing newcomers to compete.

VibeShort and StoryReel, two platforms specializing in AI-generated short dramas, both ranked among the top 15 overseas micro-short drama apps by revenue in the first nine months of this year, according to the latest DataEye figures.

Both apps launched in the first half of this year and reached the industry's first tier within about six months, highlighting how quickly newcomers can gain ground.

Audience Acceptance Remains a Challenge

But while producers are embracing AI, overseas audiences remain harder to convince.

Sandy Chen, YouTube's head of strategic content partnerships in China, said global audiences have not fully embraced AI-generated content, with some users explicitly expressing dissatisfaction with AI productions.

Nan also noted that overseas users are generally less receptive to AI-generated content than their counterparts in China. That leaves platforms facing a crucial test: whether lower production costs can translate into content viewers are willing to pay for.

Editor: Emmi Laine

data.title: [APFF 2026] AI Boom Spurs Trillion-Dollar Digital Infrastructure Financing Needs in Asia-Pacific, APFF Coordinator Says
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 23 -- The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence across industries is reshaping capital allocation in the Asia-Pacific region, driving digital infrastructure financing needs from billions of dollars to trillions of dollars, according to Julius Caesar Parreñas, coordinator of the Asia-Pacific Financial Forum in Hong Kong concluded yesterday.

Digital infrastructure has long required financing to support cloud services for technology companies such as US e-commerce giant Amazon, but AI has dramatically increased the scale of investment needed, Parreñas, who is also managing director at Japanese lender Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp., said in an interview with Yicai during the APFF yesterday.

"Now, instead of billions of dollars, we are talking about trillions of dollars that are needed to finance digital infrastructure and this is just for data centers," Parreñas said. "We are not yet talking about the foundational infrastructure needed for these data centers to function, like energy. You need a lot of investment in energy infrastructure, also water, and of course, human resources."

The financing needs have become a key issue for regional policymakers and were discussed at a recent working lunch between Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation finance ministers and the APEC Business Advisory Council, he said.

Hong Kong's Role

Parreñas highlighted Hong Kong's efforts to adapt its policy and regulatory environment to digital finance, saying the city was playing a leading role in the region.

"Hong Kong is undertaking a lot of reforms and playing a leading role in adjusting the policy and regulatory environment for the digital world," he said.

Hong Kong's close ties with mainland China and its connections with other regional economies put it in a position to help advance digital transformation across the Asia-Pacific, he added. The special administrative region also has an opportunity to establish standards and best practices and connect APEC member economies with one another and with markets beyond the region, he said.

"There is a big opportunity for Hong Kong to play a leading role in establishing standards, in establishing best practices, and then actually connecting to the other member economies of APEC and beyond," he said.

Beyond AI

Parreñas also discussed APFF's role in advancing financial reform across the region. "What we want to see is actual reforms taking place," he said.

One example is efforts to broaden the assets that small and medium-sized enterprises can use as loan collateral. In many Asian economies, banks have traditionally relied on real estate, leaving SMEs that have assets such as accounts receivable, inventories and intellectual property with fewer options for securing loans.

APEC finance ministers included movable-asset collateral reform as a top priority under the Cebu Action Plan in 2015. APFF subsequently brought international experts to advise policymakers on legal and regulatory changes. The Philippines completed its reform in 2018, and Brunei Darussalam also pursued reforms. In mainland China, the People's Bank of China invited APFF to hold workshops for those drafting the secured-transactions chapter of the Civil Code.

"A lot of things that we advocated actually went into the reform," Parreñas said.

APFF operates on a "demand-driven" basis, he added, and hopes more APEC member economies will seek its assistance in implementing policy priorities set by finance ministers.

Editor: Kim Taylor

data.title: Chinese Online Sellers Ramp Up Inventories for Holiday Shopping Season as Trade Risks Mount
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 23 -- Chinese cross-border e-commerce merchants are boosting inventories ahead of major year-end shopping events despite mounting trade uncertainties and longer shipping times.

Inventory stocked in overseas warehouses by merchants on Alibaba Group Holding's AliExpress platform has surged 146 percent from a year earlier ahead of Double 11, China's biggest annual online shopping event that culminates on Nov. 11, and Christmas, according to data provided by the platform.

AliExpress operates overseas warehouses in six countries: Spain, France, Poland, Germany, the United States, and South Korea. Despite trade uncertainties, merchants are stocking up earlier to meet holiday demand, reflecting confidence in overseas markets.

Stocking Earlier to Capture Overseas Demand

Some exporters see greater risks in running out of stock than in holding excess inventory.

Maintaining sufficient inventories is even more important amid growing trade uncertainties, as having products readily available creates more opportunities to expand overseas, Huang Zhijin, head of e-commerce at Bear Electric Appliance's overseas business unit, told Yicai. Foshan-based Bear makes kitchen appliances and baby care products.

Despite frequent changes in trade policies, Bear has achieved significant sales growth in its main overseas market, the US, this year, although the pace has been slightly slower than expected, Huang said. Sales in some other countries have exceeded expectations.

The company's overall overseas sales are expected to grow by double digits this year, reinforcing Huang's belief that “as long as there is stock, there are many possibilities.”

Longer shipping times are also forcing merchants to plan further ahead. Rockbros, a Chinese cycling gear brand, began stocking up in April for year-end overseas shopping promotions because of longer sea freight transit times, founder David Zhang told Yicai.

Zhang said the company now stocks up at least three months in advance, compared with two months previously, to ensure shipments reach overseas warehouses before sales promotions begin.

Overseas markets are Rockbros' main business focus this year, Zhang said. In addition to selling products through cross-border e-commerce platforms, the company is developing a network of physical specialty stores in its target markets.

Rockbros expects its overall overseas business to grow more than 20 percent this year, while sales on AliExpress during Double 11 are projected to surge by more than half, Zhang added.

GameSir, a Chinese gaming equipment brand, has taken an even more aggressive approach to inventory planning.

The developer of game controllers and software has stocked at least USD5 million worth of products for overseas markets this year, exceeding its USD4 million sales target, Partner Lian You told Yicai.

GameSir has also extended its inventory preparation period to nearly four months from the previous one to two months to ensure sufficient supplies in overseas warehouses if demand surges.

Lian said demand for the company's products remains strong despite trade policy uncertainties, making sufficient inventories essential to meeting overseas customer needs.

Localization and Compliance Support Expansion

Chinese exporters are also tailoring their operations to local markets.

Bear's Huang said consumers worldwide share a demand for high-quality products, but purchasing habits and product preferences vary significantly across countries.

For example, Chinese consumers are generally willing to wait seven to nine minutes for an electric kettle to boil water, while British consumers expect the process to take just three minutes, Huang noted. Kettles sold in the United Kingdom therefore need higher power output.

To advance its localization strategy, Bear established an office in the US this year and is developing production capacity in several emerging markets, Huang said.

Compliance is the home appliance company's top priority when expanding overseas and must be addressed well in advance, he added.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Emmi Laine

data.title: [APFF 2026] IIPCC President Calls for Shift From IP Trading to IP Commercialization
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 23 -- The focus on intellectual property should shift from trading to commercialization, enabling businesses to generate value from patents, trademarks, and other IPs in more ways, according to Michael Lin, president of the International IP Commercialization Council.

Shifting from IP trading to IP commercialization should be the first step, while the second one should be opening up areas where people can make money from IPs in different ways, Lin, who coordinates the Asia-Pacific Financial Forum's IP Finance Working Group, told Yicai in an interview.

A US patent attorney who has worked in Asia for 30 years and has been based in Hong Kong for the past 16 years also explored the challenges of commercializing academic research, the role of valuation in IP financing, and the importance of understanding local markets when Chinese companies expand overseas.

Excerpts from the interview with Lin are below:

Yicai: You work closely with university spin-outs and scientists. What separates IPs that can attract financing from those that remain difficult to commercialize?

Michael Lin: A lot of the IPs that I see are not commercialized simply because they are too far upstream. I work with a lot of university spin-outs and professors. They're world-class scientists and know their science and technology better than anyone else. But if you're saying ‘I'm gonna use this technology, and I'm gonna cure cancer,’ that's a 25 to 35 year research project. The patent will probably expire by the time you actually get this to market, if you ever get it to market, and the failure rate is 90 percent anyway. So that is something which is very, very difficult to commercialize. It's almost impossible to get investment for.

What a lot of professors and spin-outs need to think about is: here's the 35-year end goal, but how can I make money to support my research along the way? What products or services, such as reagents, stem cell lines, or cancer cell lines, can they make and sell now to fund the next 35 years of research?

That is how you reposition the invention so you can actually attract investment and commercialize it.

Yicai: IP valuation is frequently cited as a major bottleneck in IP financing. Why do banks and investors struggle to trust IP valuations, and how can this be fixed?

Lin: I really love the valuation people. There are a lot of them. They even admit that sometimes, when they provide a valuation, the people requesting it aren't doing the right thing with it. Valuation is good for certain things, but if you use it for something else just because it's a number, you may not be using it right.

If you have a startup doing a product line like I was talking about curing cancer, the valuation is gonna be very, very low. I can take this patent and say, for a startup, it's worth HKD1 million (USD127,530), but for Sanofi or Roche, if it's going to be that one piece of IP which makes them win the court case against the other, this is worth USD200 million or USD300 million, not Hong Kong dollars.

There's a lot of misunderstanding about what valuation is and why it's being used, and I think education is a big part of it. The message is lost when you start talking to the finance people and the bankers and other people who are actually going to use the valuation for valuing this loan or something like that.

Yicai: Hong Kong has been promoting itself as a regional hub for IP for years. What conditions are needed for a mature IP financing and commercialization market to grow here?

Lin: Hong Kong has been doing this for at least since I got here, which is 16 years. But I think that the first thing they need to do is change the name. It's not IP trading they've been talking about.

Trading implies that things are of equal value. IP is by definition unique. A trademark for IIPCC, as much as I love it and think it's a great organization, doesn't have the same value as the Apple trademark, the Huawei trademark, or the Tencent trademark, since those are worth billions of US dollars. One patent is not the same as another. But to finance people, to accountants, one patent is one patent, one trademark is one trademark. They think everything is fungible, and it's not. So there's a need for education, but I also think understanding the economics of IP matters too, because again, it's not the IP, it's what you do with the IP.

That's why the IP trading hub has had such huge difficulties. For the most part, there's no secondary market in most IPs right now. The closest thing you actually have to a secondary market in IP is domain names, an open market where you can bid on them.

So the first thing I would do is change it from IP trading to IP commercialization. Then you open up a lot of different areas where people can make money from the IP in different ways. Frankly, I think that we should overcome a lot of the business bias against the term 'IP trading.' IP commercialization is much more accurate, and I think it has much broader appeal.

Yicai: As more Chinese technology and manufacturing companies expand globally, what are the biggest IP and commercialization challenges they face beyond the technology itself?

Lin: The IP itself is useless unless you're gonna do something with it. There are many things you can do with it, and they vary widely from one economy to another.

Brand recognition alone can vary sharply by market. "BMW's trademark is worth a lot in the US and in Europe, but in China they have a different name for it, which is Baoma.

It's often not just one technology, but a combination of the technology, the brand, the sourcing, the reputation of the company, the goodwill, the trade secrets. I know a lot of places where my friends say: 'Oh, we love buying Chinese products. They're higher quality than our local products.’ So they sell for a premium. Whereas in China, they're just very, very competitive with all the other Chinese products.

Chinese companies looking to expand overseas need to investigate the local market, laws, regulations, and economic conditions, then adjust their business accordingly. You could gain a huge advantage, or it could be a disadvantage if you don't understand what's going on.

Editor: Futura Costaglione

data.title: Chinese AI Short Drama Stocks Rise Amid Intensifying Performance Divergence
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 23 -- Stocks of Chinese firms in the artificial intelligence short drama market have surged this month amid growing investor interest, but while some report solid profits from the business, others say it has yet to generate revenue and contributes only a small part to overall performance.

Shares of television program producer Ciwen Media Group [SHE: 002343] and film and television drama distributor H&R Century Union [SHE: 000892] have surged by their daily trading limit for several consecutive days, with the former ending up 10 percent at CNY10.89 (USD11.63) in Shenzhen today, while the latter fell 0.2 percent to CNY4.40 (66 US cents). Several other companies have also seen abnormal stock trading fluctuations after reporting on ongoing AI short drama businesses.

Despite plunging 8.6 percent to HKD1.02 (13 US cents) a share as of 3.20 p.m. in Hong Kong, Duiba Group’s stock [HKG: 1753] remains up 625 percent since Aug. 21. On Oct. 14, the Hangzhou-based company said it expects its AI short drama business to have been profitable in July, August, and September.

Shares of Decai Decoration [SHA: 605287] ended 1.6 percent higher at CNY42.30 apiece in Shanghai, bringing the monthly gain to 19.4 percent. On Oct. 12, the firm cited reports that its holding subsidiary is involved in AI comic drama production, but said the business is still in its early stages, with relatively low revenue and ongoing losses.

However, different segments in the AI short drama market are increasingly diverging, with pricing power centered on those that control traffic distribution channels, high-quality intellectual property reserves, and the underlying AI computing infrastructure, Guo Tao, an angel investor and AI expert, told Yicai. Platform operators control traffic-bidding rules and revenue-sharing settlement systems, making them the core party dictating profit allocation, Guo said.

In addition, industry price wars are disrupting the profitability of compute and AI tool providers, Guo stressed. By contrast, traditional production teams operate on a project basis, with their revenue and profits heavily depending on the performance of individual short dramas, making their bargaining power relatively weak and leading to risks related to computing power, traffic acquisition, and script development, which results in highly volatile profitability, Guo pointed out.

The number of AI short drama users in China surpassed 600 million in the first half of this year, while the market is expected to surge 138 percent to over CNY40 billion (USD6 billion) this year from the previous year, according to a report by DataEye. Users also show strong willingness to pay for AI short dramas, with more than half of 1,000 survey respondents saying they had previously paid for such content.

User demand and commercial potential have grown, but supply is expanding even faster. In the first half of the year, ByteDance’s short-video platform Douyin added about 221,900 AI short and comic dramas. However, only 1,055 surpassed 100 million views, with more than 90 percent running at a loss using 50 million views as the break-even level.

“The winner-takes-most effect in the AI short drama market will continue to intensify,” Guo said. On the supply side, the benefits of AI in significantly lowering production barriers are being offset by the rapid expansion of content supply, while traffic-bidding costs continue to rise, Guo noted.

This is also why service providers like Duiba, which focus on short drama distribution matchmaking and paid monetization, are more likely to deliver short-term profits, Guo pointed out, adding that for ordinary production teams, the challenge of how to diversify the risk of failure for individual projects and capture more value across the supply chain is becoming increasingly severe.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: Chinese LLM Firms Launch Double 11 Campaigns to Boost Token Awareness
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 23 -- Tokens from leading Chinese large language model developers have entered the Double 11 shopping festival for the first time this year, but unlike the big discounts most products enjoy, token prices remain largely unchanged, with promotional campaigns seemingly more focused on using the event's popularity to secure an entry point into the market.

E-commerce platforms have been aggressively pursuing LLM developers to join them for the shopping festival, making "buy tokens on Double 11" one of their main selling points. Alibaba Group Holding's Tmall Group launched the "Artificial Intelligence Space" token recharge center last month, with Z.AI, Alibaba Cloud, and QwenWork opening stores, before MiniMax Group joined on Oct. 13. In addition, JD.Com launched its Double 11 AI token service section, attracting DeepSeek, Z.AI's GLM, and Volcano Engine's Seed among others, while Z.AI also opened a self-operated flagship store.

However, instead of "boosting token sales," e-commerce platforms have mostly focused on letting consumers know that "tokens are sold." JD.Com's self-operated flagship store for JD Cloud, MiniMax's flagship shop on Tmall, and Alibaba Cloud's official flagship store have not yet sold tokens during the festival, multiple customers told Yicai.

The price of the monthly card for Z.AI's GLM Coding Plan Lite on JD.Com dropped to CNY115 from CNY118 (USD17.22 from USD17.67) for Double 11, and fell even less on Tmall, where it stands at CNY116.90.

In addition, Tmall will not offer any specific vouchers for tokens for the time being, said President Jia Luo.

In the past, e-commerce sites subsidized brands that did not lower prices during Double 11, such as Apple, often using their platform subsidies and category vouchers to lower prices on related products.

Token sales on Alibaba's Taobao surged 450 percent on the first day of Double 11 from the previous month's average but remained low. The page information for Z.AI's GLM Coding Plan Lite on JD.Com showed only "over 100 sold" for the monthly card, while total sales of all tokens on Z.AI's flagship store on Tmall reached 300, and on MiniMax's shop just over 100 tokens.

Tokens still target a specific, limited set of customers and have not yet reached the explosive potential of mass consumer goods, Orient Securities pointed out. LLM pricing methods began to differentiate this year, with prices for homogeneous general models declining while high-end models with complex reasoning abilities are starting to command premiums.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: Europe-China Business Fair Opens as Small Cities Forge New Ties
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- The 19th Europe-China Business and Technology Cooperation Fair opened in Chengdu today, bringing together European and Chinese businesses and local governments to forge closer economic ties.

Delegations from more than 20 European countries and regions are attending the event, according to the China Chamber of International Commerce. The fair aims to deepen cooperation between smaller cities and businesses by connecting industries with complementary strengths.

Among those seeking new partnerships is Loja, a small town in southern Spain. Led by Mayor Joaquín Ordóñez Gámez, its delegation brings together producers of extra virgin olive oil and cured ham alongside businesses in cold-chain logistics, bulk commodities and aviation technical services.

The Loja delegation signed a letter of intent to establish friendly cooperative ties with Pengzhou, a county-level city in Sichuan province, on its first day in Chengdu, laying the groundwork for cooperation between their complementary industries.

Located in Spain's Andalusia region, Loja has a population of about 20,000. Its main industries include extra virgin olive oil and cured ham production, and the town is also home to the indigenous Lojeña sheep breed.

The two cities also share an interest in caviar production. Loja has what is described as the world's first technology for extracting and processing organic caviar without surgically opening the fish, while Pengzhou accounts for about 14 percent of global caviar output, Yicai learned.

“Many small European cities have substantial demand for cooperation that has yet to be fully recognized," Duan Lian, Chinese secretary-general of the Sino-European Industrial Innovation Promotion Association and an advisor on Chinese affairs to Loja, told Yicai. "Targeted partnerships between the specialized industries of smaller cities on both sides could unlock enormous potential for practical cooperation.”

Untapped Potential in China's Consumer Market

Liam Jia, team lead of the EU SME Center, said European companies across most industries still have considerable untapped opportunities in the Chinese market.

“A typical real-world example: China ranks as the world’s largest honey producer, yet many small European SMEs successfully sell high-end specialty honey into the Chinese market," Jia said, adding that affluent Chinese consumers are willing to pay more for distinctive flavors and superior quality.

Chinese consumers are still becoming familiar with premium Spanish cured ham, according to Verónica Manchón Moreno, marketing director at Spanish ham producer Lizana, which is preparing to enter the Chinese market.

Moreno said the company plans to win over Chinese buyers by highlighting its production standards and animal welfare practices, explaining what sets its products apart and justifies their prices.

Beyond selling olive oil and cured ham to China, Loja is seeking partnerships with Chinese companies in solar power, energy storage and smart agriculture, Mayor Ordóñez said.

The town is also exploring partnerships with Chinese investors in tourism to develop resort projects incorporating traditional Chinese medicine and wellness services, he added.

China-EU cooperation should not be confined to large corporations and major cities, but should also extend to thousands of smaller Spanish towns such as Loja and their counterparts across China, the mayor concluded.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Emmi Laine

data.title: Shanghai Port Advances Green Shipping Push With Hamburg, Melbourne
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- The Port of Shanghai, the world’s busiest container port, is accelerating its green transition by expanding clean marine fuel supplies and developing green shipping corridors with major international ports across Europe, and Australia.

The Chinese port can now provide ship-to-ship bunkering of bonded liquefied natural gas and green methanol, while advancing cleaner shipping routes, Yicai learned at the 2026 North Bund Forum, which ended yesterday.

At the event, Shanghai unveiled development goals and a roadmap for a green shipping corridor with Germany's Hamburg, along with an outline implementation plan for a similar corridor with Australia's Melbourne. The announcements build on its existing cooperation with Los Angeles and Long Beach in California.

Shanghai's initiatives support the shipping industry's push to achieve the International Maritime Organization's target of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions around 2050. Its efforts also include expanding shore power and reducing diesel use at container terminals.

Shipping carries more than four-fifths of global trade by volume, but its vast scale and reliance on fossil fuels make decarbonization a major challenge. The shift to alternative fuels such as LNG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, and electricity requires not only new propulsion systems but also changes to fuel infrastructure, ship design, port operations, crew training, and international trade rules.

Shanghai Port Emerges as Global Green Shipping Model

A key part of Shanghai's green transition is reducing emissions from ships while in port.

Shore power allows berthed vessels to draw electricity from port grids instead of running fuel-powered generators, cutting fuel consumption and emissions, particularly when renewable energy is used.

Shore power facilities now cover more than 90 percent of Chinese ports and over 98 percent of ports along the Yangtze River Economic Belt, according to Gu Jinshan, president of the China Ports and Harbors Association, a national port industry group.

Shore power use by ships during port calls has quadrupled compared with 2020, while a green shore power corridor stretching from Chongqing to Shanghai is helping promote cleaner port operations, Gu said.

Shanghai is also shifting away from diesel at its container terminals, moving toward greater use of electricity, LNG, and renewable power. Diesel's share of energy consumption fell to 13 percent at the end of 2025 from 47 percent in 2015, according to Gu.

Beyond port operations, Shanghai is expanding its supply of cleaner marine fuels to help oceangoing vessels cut emissions.

Green methanol bunkering volumes at the Port of Shanghai have approached 40,000 tons so far this year. Bonded LNG bunkering reached 771,000 cubic meters last year, with volumes expected to surpass that level this year.

The port's international partnerships are also taking shape. At last year's North Bund Forum, Shanghai and the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach unveiled the results of their cooperation on a green shipping corridor. The latest plans for corridors with Hamburg and Melbourne extend those efforts to Europe and Australia.

Eugene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, told Yicai that cutting emissions from ships traveling between Shanghai and Los Angeles by just 10 percent would be equivalent to eliminating an entire year's pollution at the Port of Los Angeles.

Seroka also said the port's business with China has grown steadily since March, accounting for more than 40 percent of its total business. September marked the port's strongest monthly performance in its 118-year history, while container throughput approached three million twenty-foot equivalent units in the third quarter.

Green Transition Reshapes Shipbuilding and Port Industries

The growing adoption of alternative marine fuels is also transforming the shipbuilding industry.

As shipowners turn to alternative fuels, shipyards must adapt engines, storage tanks, pipelines, and safety systems to different fuel requirements. The shift presents both technical challenges and new business opportunities as competing propulsion technologies reshape the shipbuilding market.

Vessel leasing company COSCO Shipping Development owns or has on order more than 100 dual-fuel green vessels with a combined capacity of 14 million deadweight tons, according to General Manager Wang Kunhui.

These include methanol- and LNG-capable vessels, giving the company a more diversified alternative-fuel fleet and orderbook, Wang said.

Existing ships can also cut fuel consumption without replacing their propulsion systems. Brian Adrian Wessel, director general of the Danish Maritime Authority, said targeted efficiency improvements based on assessments of operations and available technologies can deliver significant savings.

For example, a bulk carrier built in 2009 could save almost 1,810 tons of fuel annually, equivalent to about 18 percent of its previous consumption, by optimizing its sailing speed, routes, equipment, and operational management, he said.

The transition could also reshape the role of ports. Gu of the CPHA said developing zero-carbon terminals and port areas will require closer integration of energy supplies, transportation, operations, and management.

As demand for green marine fuels grows, ports could evolve from energy consumers into energy suppliers and service providers, creating business opportunities in fuel storage, transportation, bunkering, safety management, and trading, he added.

Editor: Emmi Laine

data.title: China’s Chip Talent Market Splits as Experience Trumps Degrees
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- China’s semiconductor industry continues to face a significant talent shortage, driving up salaries for specialized roles. Yet a growing pool of university graduates and stricter experience requirements are making it harder for entry-level candidates to find suitable jobs, industry insiders told Yicai.

Demand is growing fastest for chip design roles related to artificial intelligence, such as central processing unit, graphics processing unit and neural processing unit positions, a senior headhunter told Yicai.

Other fast-growing areas include memory chips, optical chips and optical communications, all of which are closely linked to computing power, he said. By contrast, demand for semiconductor talent in traditional sectors such as consumer electronics and security systems has remained relatively stable.

The number of new job postings in the chip industry soared 22.2 percent in the first nine months from a year earlier, according to the latest industry data obtained by Yicai from Liepin. The average annual salary offered for these positions jumped 8.8 percent year on year to CNY291,900 (USD43,738).

Demand for talent specializing in Chiplet technology, in particular, has surged. Chiplet is a chip architecture in which multiple smaller chips, known as chiplets, are manufactured separately and then integrated into a single unit through advanced packaging techniques.

The number of newly advertised Chiplet-related positions soared 211.2 percent year on year, and has increased by a cumulative 451.4 percent over the past two years. The average annual salary offered is now more than double the industry average for the chip sector at CNY649,500 (USD97,335). Job openings in advanced packaging also rose sharply, increasing 134.6 percent year on year, with an average annual salary of CNY422,400 (USD63,300).

Shanghai Enflame Technology recently offered an “astronomical” salary of up to CNY1.8 million (USD269,715) a year for a Chiplet D2D AI chip architect position. D2D stands for Die-to-Die, which refers to the interconnection technology that enables individual chiplets to communicate with one another.

Behind the rapid rise in salaries is a very small pool of qualified candidates. Enflame’s “astronomical-salary” position requires applicants to have more than 10 years of experience in chip architecture.

“Across the country, there are probably only about 200 to 300 people who truly meet this requirement, and most of them have already been snapped up by leading companies,” an insider at a listed AI chipmaker told Yicai. “This is because most Chiplet projects in China are still at the early stages of architecture definition or verification, leaving few candidates with the required decade or more of experience.”

Graduate Job Squeeze

The broader trend of firms offering high salaries to attract top-tier talent has done little to improve job prospects for recent graduates from semiconductor-related programs.

A recent doctoral graduate in microelectronics from a well-known university told Yicai that the number of graduates majoring in semiconductor-related fields has surged over the past two years. Companies have responded by raising their requirements for industry experience, making it significantly more difficult for fresh graduates to find jobs.

“Four years ago, graduates from semiconductor-related programs at top universities could secure job offers very quickly. But as firms receive more applications, the advantage of having a prestigious university on one’s resume is diminishing, while employers are imposing increasingly stringent requirements for specialized, directly relevant experience,” the person said.

Building expertise in the semiconductor industry takes a long time. Engineers typically need three to five years of project experience to develop into fully capable professionals, making it difficult for fresh graduates and applicants from other fields to take on core research and development roles in the short term, said Wang Pan, co-founder of Thorsianway Microelectronics Technology.

Among chip industry job postings from January to September, positions requiring three to five years of work experience accounted for 31.86 percent of the total, according to Liepin data. Those requiring five to 10 years of experience accounted for 30.48 percent, making it the fastest-growing experience bracket year on year.

Specialist Talent Shortages

Several industry insiders interviewed by Yicai expect competition for semiconductor jobs to intensify, particularly at the entry level. Meanwhile, companies will continue to compete aggressively for AI chip architects and senior engineers with three to five years of relevant experience.

“Over the next three to five years, the most acute talent shortages will be concentrated in three areas, namely D2D/C2C interconnect protocols and proprietary IP development, high-bandwidth memory interface design and system-level architecture optimization driven by AI workloads,” the insider at the listed AI chipmaker said.

The shortage of professionals skilled in full-stack chip design, 3D stacking and advanced packaging is likely to persist over the long term, he added.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Kim Taylor

data.title: Chinese Scientists Use Shanghai AI Lab's Scientific Model to Solve First World-Class Match Problem
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 16 -- A research team led by Xu Disheng, a professor at Great Bay University, has used a scientific multimodal artificial intelligence model developed by Shanghai AI Laboratory to prove the three-dimensional Ghys conjecture, marking the first time a domestic AI model has solved a world-class mathematical problem.

The proof of the Ghys conjecture, which has puzzled the mathematical community for 30 years, was completed using Intern-S2, Shanghai AI Lab announced yesterday. A team led by Dong Bin, a professor at Peking University, and Liu Ruochuan, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, has verified the findings, it added.

The paper on the proof has been published on the preprint platform arXiv, while the formal code was made available to the public on the code-sharing platform GitHub.

The Ghys conjecture, proposed by French mathematician Etienne Ghys in 1995, asks whether the behavior of chaotic dynamical systems can determine their geometric classification. It has long been regarded as a key open question in dynamical systems and a benchmark for testing mathematical reasoning capabilities.

A student of Fields Medal winner Artur Avila, Xu has long committed to proving the Ghys conjecture. After noticing the potential of AI models in math research last year, he visited the Shanghai AI Lab and formed a team that began collaborative research on model training at the start of this year.

Intern-S2, the result of the team upgrading the previous-generation Intern-S1, began exploring the Ghys conjecture from multiple angles in August, producing thousands of pages of derivations, based on which Xu and his partners continuously provided feedback to the model, corrected reverse exploration‌, and successfully found the proof method through multiple rounds of human-computer interaction.

The significance of this study lies in verifying a new scientific research paradigm, which is different from traditional math research that relies on long exploration by individual geniuses, Shanghai AI Lab pointed out. The proof systematically integrates expert intuition into the computer solving loop and creates a closed loop of "system exploration -- expert judgment -- achievement accumulation -- feedback correction," it added.

This paradigm can be replicated and used in more basic research fields with "huge search space but scarce experts" to achieve more original innovation breakthroughs from 0 to 1, the lab stressed.

AI's role in math research has attracted widespread attention. OpenAI said it spent 88 hours using 10,000 AI agents to solve the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem last month, while releasing 722 mathematical manuscripts covering multiple fields, including number theory, geometry, and algebra, earlier this month.

However, OpenAI's radical attempts have sparked controversy within the industry. After the US firm announced a proof of the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, 25 Fields Medal winners, including Terence Chi-Shen Tao and Deng Yu, said that AI companies treat solving math problems as benchmark tests, which harms the mathematical community.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: China Puts First Satellite of World’s First Low-Inclination Remote Sensing Constellation Into Orbit
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- The first satellite of the Wuyang Constellation, the world’s first low-inclination remote sensing constellation, was successfully launched into a 541-kilometer low Earth orbit to monitor the natural environment in low-latitude regions.

Galactic Energy sent the Xiguang-4 01 satellite, made by Xi’an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics CAS Aerospace Science and Technology Group, into space on its Ceres-1 sea-launch rocket from near eastern Shandong province yesterday.

The Wuyang Constellation innovatively adopts a non-sun-synchronous, low-inclination orbit design and provides targeted services to the low-latitude region between 35 degrees north and south latitude, said Gu Xingfa, chief engineer of the project and director of the Institute of Aerospace Remote Sensing Innovations at Guangzhou University. It is designed to have a network of three pioneer satellites and 25 business satellites, Gu added.

The global earth observation industry has long been dominated by sun-synchronous polar orbit satellites, with observation resources and capabilities tilted towards mid to high latitudes, resulting in great shortcomings in remote sensing observations in low latitude regions between 35 degrees north and south latitude, including coverage blind spots and a shortage of quantitative remote sensing data supply, Gu pointed out.

The Wuyang Constellation is expected to become China’s first smart aerospace information service system for low-latitude areas, providing services for regular monitoring, refined management, and rapid emergency response of the natural environment in such regions, Gu stressed.

As the constellation’s pioneer satellite, Xiguang-4 01 will carry out key missions of orbit system verification, remote sensing payload assessment, new technology verification, and multi-scenario application demonstration, according to Xi’an Institute of Optics.

After entering orbit, Xiguang-4 01 will support various scenarios, including natural resource monitoring, agricultural production, ocean observation, ecological protection, flood and typhoon emergency disaster reduction, and urban governance in low-latitude regions in South China and along the Maritime Silk Road. It will likely offer unique monitoring advantages for typhoons, red tides, crop growth, and urban agglomeration expansion, among others.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Martin Kadiev

data.title: China’s Chery Auto to Become AI-Driven Smart Tech Firm by 2035, Chairman Says
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- Chinese carmaker Chery Automobile has set a goal to turn into an “artificial intelligence-driven global intelligent technology company” over the next 10 years, according to its chairman.

At the Chery Global Innovation Conference held in Wuhu on Oct. 20, Yin Tongyue said he is happy to hear people often say the company’s cars are becoming less and less like cars and Chery is becoming less and less an automaker.

The conference was held at Chery’s Global R&D Center under the theme “Change -- Using AI to Reshape a Better World, Let Life Return to Life,” with autos making up only one part of the many products on display.

Among the 11 core technological achievements released at the event, several went beyond complete vehicles. Chery is applying auto technologies to its AiMOGA humanoid robots, robotaxis, electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, energy, and agricultural machinery.

Chery backs the launch of new technologies through continuous increases in research and development spending. The firm’s R&D expenditure jumped 28 percent to CNY6.7 billion (USD1 billion) in the first half of this year from a year earlier, according to its financial report.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Martin Kadiev

data.title: Born Global, Embarking Anew: Yicai Global Ushers in the Next Decade
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- On its 10th anniversary, Yicai Global, the English-language new media brand of Yicai Media Group, has unveiled MAPS, its development strategy for the next decade, aiming to speed up the shift from ‘Made in China, distributed globally’ to ‘made globally, delivered globally.’ MAPS stands for Matrix, Artificial Intelligence, Pivot, and Service.

To understand this strategy, one must understand the era we live in. Global coverage of China reached 6.68 million articles in 2025, a four-year high, according to the China in the Eyes of Global Media big-data analysis report, which Yicai Global has published for four consecutive years. Positive coverage continues to account for a larger share and to grow faster than negative coverage.

China’s innovation capacity is shifting from “an object of doubt” to “a subject of study,” and the country is increasingly seen as an important force shaping global supply chains, financial markets, and technological innovation. However, greater attention also means closer scrutiny, as every step China takes is put under the microscope.

Against this backdrop, when the world wants to understand China, a question arises for Chinese financial media: are their sources truthful and complete enough, and can a credible professional media organization deliver that content to global readers?

Meanwhile, AI is transforming the entire chain of content production and distribution, the global media landscape is being rapidly reshuffled, and many Chinese companies going global are entering a new, more systematic, and in-depth phase.

Yicai began its global expansion when it was founded in 2003. From the start, it worked with CNBC and other leading international media outlets to produce English-language news programs, and it set up bureaus and studios in major global economic and financial centers. In 2016, it launched Yicai Global as its English-language new media brand, using English as a bridge to report on China’s economy for a global audience.

Through exclusive interviews with global political and business leaders and heads of international organizations, Yicai Global reporters have made the brand an important reference for international investors and decision-makers assessing China’s trends. Its content now reaches more than 180 countries and regions, with more than 250 million original page views and 10,000 citations a year by leading overseas media.

During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), Yicai Global’s content was cited 131,000 times by overseas think tanks, blogs, and social media opinion leaders. Overseas large language models recommend it as a reliable source.

Shanghai, where Yicai is headquartered, is a key hub connecting China with the world and an important vantage point from which the world observes China. Its 15th Five-Year Plan explicitly calls for strengthening international communication capacity.

On the technology side, Yicai Global already has a self-developed LLM for finance and AI agents that serve Chinese companies going global. It also has a communication matrix covering major global social media platforms and a dialogue platform for senior global audiences.

Yicai Global will remain committed to being objective, rational, professional, and fact-based, express China’s position on global financial issues, and use truthful, comprehensive, and accurate newsgathering to respond to outside concerns.

The author of this article is Sun Ji, director of Yicai Global.

Editor: Futura Costaglione

data.title: First Fuel From Goldwind's Green Hydrogen Project in Inner Mongolia Is Shipped Overseas
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- China's green hydrogen sector is entering the commercial proof stage, where it can be assessed and financed, with the first batch of bio-methanol from a project by Chinese wind turbine maker Goldwind Science & Technology in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region delivered to the Port of Busan in South Korea.

The first of Hydrexia Holding's hydrogen production plants at Goldwind's green methanol project in Xing'an League has been operating stably, the Shanghai-based integrated hydrogen technology solution provider announced at the Green Fuel Industry Forum on Oct. 19. Relevant bio-methanol has been used to refuel ships in Busan, it added.

Goldwind's project uses wind power to produce hydrogen and couples it with biomass gasification to boost green methanol production, with a total planned output of 1.45 million tons and a 250,000-ton Phase I capacity already in operation. Hydrexia is the core technology and equipment supplier for its hydrogen production segment.

Beijing-based Goldwind has signed long-term green methanol supply guarantee agreements for more than 850,000 tons with Denmark's Maersk, Germany's Hapag-Lloyd, and Japan's Ocean Network Express Holdings. Last month, the project's first batch of products completed international certification.

Behind the commercialization boost lies the economics validated through large-scale industrial operation. Yao Changsheng, chairman of Hydrexia, said that with the launch of next-generation hydrogen electrolysis products, the company can reduce the levelized cost of green hydrogen to CNY10 to CNY12 (USD1.50 to USD1.80) per kilogram.

In addition, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology recently issued a document organizing the implementation of four pilot tasks for comprehensive hydrogen energy applications: hydrogen energy technology and equipment research and development, industrial hydrogen energy projects, promotion of fuel cell vehicles, and building hydrogen refueling stations.

The new policy focus is expanding from fuel cell vehicles to developing a supply-and-demand system, coordinating the promotion of large-scale hydrogen energy applications across equipment manufacturing, green hydrogen production and sales, and supporting infrastructure, while also exploring a commercial closed loop, an executive at an electrolyzer company told Yicai.

China's green hydrogen market has passed its bubble period and entered a stage of steady growth, with an industry explosion expected between 2030 and 2035, said Ouyang Minggao, professor at Tsinghua University and president of the International Hydrogen Fuel Cell Association. By 2050-2060, as carbon neutrality is gradually achieved, the domestic green hydrogen market could reach 100 million to 175 million tons, accounting for 10 percent to 15 percent of terminal energy consumption, he added.

China accounts for about 30 percent of the global hydrogen production and consumption, with the country having upgraded hydrogen from a chemical raw material to a strategic resource at the legal level, noted Mikaa Blugeon-Mered, a senior expert on global hydrogen market research at the University of Quebec, adding that it has also actively laid out key midstream segments including pipeline transportation and hydrogen storage, an exploratory move ahead of the global curve.

In addition, the decarbonization in the global aviation and shipping sectors is creating robust demand for green fuels. In 2023, the International Maritime Organization adopted a new emissions reduction strategy requiring the shipping industry to cut carbon emissions by at least 20 percent (striving for 30 percent) from 2008 levels by 2030, and to reach net zero across the entire industry by 2050.

In addition, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation entered its first phase in 2024 before switching to a mandatory compliance model next year, requiring global airlines to purchase sustainable aviation fuel or carbon allowances to offset excess emissions.

According to estimates by Det Norske Veritas, driven by the European Union carbon tax, global aviation and shipping will consume a combined 34 million tons of green fuels by 2030.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: Chinese EV Giant BYD Enters Namibian Market in Global Expansion Drive
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 7 -- Chinese automaker BYD has officially launched its new energy vehicle brand in Namibia, expanding its presence in the African market.

Namibian automotive distributor Pupkewitz Motors announced yesterday that it will represent BYD in the country, with the brand to be offered through retail outlets in Windhoek, Walvis Bay and Ongwediva.

"Our ambition is not simply to introduce new vehicles to the market, but to create an experience around new energy mobility that is relevant to Namibian customers. We look forward to building awareness, educating consumers and allowing customers to experience BYD for themselves," said Nico Pieters, a franchise executive at Pupkewitz Motors, in a statement.

Models being introduced to the Namibian market include the BYD Dolphin, BYD Dolphin Surf, BYD Sealion 5, BYD Sealion 6, BYD Shark 6, BYD Sealion 7 and BYD Seal Performance.

"The range allows Namibian customers to explore different forms of electrified mobility while experiencing the technology, comfort and features associated with the BYD brand," Pieters said.

He said the launch comes as energy efficiency, sustainability and the future of transportation gain increasing attention globally.

"BYD's global focus on new energy technologies places the brand at the forefront of this changing automotive landscape, while its entry into Namibia provides local motorists with greater access to alternative vehicle technologies," he added.

With the official launch of BYD, Pupkewitz Motors is expanding its portfolio to include a global new energy vehicle brand, reinforcing its commitment to providing Namibian customers with greater choice as mobility evolves.

In September, economic and market indicators from Namibian firm IJG Securities, showed that Chinese brands are steadily gaining popularity in Namibia. Haval, Jetour and Chery accounted for 5.9 percent, 5.8 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively, of the Namibian passenger vehicle market.

Editor: Dou Shicong

data.title: Yicai Global Unveils New 10-Year Strategy With Focus on Multilingual Expansion, AI Use
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22 -- Yicai Global has unveiled its 2026-2035 strategy named MAPS (Matrix, Artificial Intelligence, Pivot, and Service), with the English-language news service of Yicai Media Group aiming to build a world-class financial communication and services platform, expand multilingual communication and AI applications, develop a global newsgathering network, and provide integrated services for Chinese companies going global and foreign firms operating in China.

In MAPS, “Matrix” focuses on multilingual global communication, “AI” on AI-enabled content production and distribution, “Pivot” on a global content ecosystem and China narrative, and “Service” on integrated services for Chinese and foreign companies, Yicai Global announced at an event marking its 10th anniversary in Shanghai yesterday.

Yicai Global plans to gradually add French, Spanish, Arabic and other languages to its content and cover major international social media platforms. It also intends to set up overseas content hubs in key regions in Europe, the Americas, and Asia and develop a round-the-clock newsgathering network across time zones, aiming to shift from producing content in China for global distribution to producing and expressing it worldwide.

Regarding AI, Yicai Global plans to build an intelligent content platform and apply AI to topic planning, multilingual translation, data analysis, and targeted distribution to improve the efficiency of content production and dissemination.

On the “Pivot” content ecosystem, Yicai Global will draw on its reporting, observations from global opinion leaders, and the professional experience of international media, financial institutions, and companies to refine its content sources and narrative framework, so that more Chinese perspectives enter global financial discussions.

The service business will center on Chinese companies expanding overseas and foreign firms deepening their presence in China. Yicai Global plans to work with partners to integrate communication, research, consulting, events, and resource-matching capabilities, offering services that cover brand communication, market insight, and business expansion.

Yicai Global also launched joint projects with several institutions and companies at the event, including Hongqiao Overseas Development Service Center, iMpact, Fudan University School of Management, UOB China, the Abu Dhabi Department of Economic Development, CNBC, and ChuHai GO.

The World Media on China report, based on four consecutive years of Yicai Global data analysis and released at the event, reviewed trends and narrative features in international media coverage of China, providing data to help assess the country’s image in the international public opinion arena.

The event also featured two roundtable discussions on the globalization and multinational operations of Chinese companies, exploring what they can learn from multinationals’ experience when going global, as well as the relationship between international communication and the narrative and brand building of Chinese enterprise globalization.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: Chinese P2P Pioneer CreditEase Asks Some Financial Advisors to Return Up to USD3 Million in Commissions, Source Says
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 22-- CreditEase, one of China's first peer-to-peer lending platforms, has sent text messages requesting commission refunds from multiple financial advisors, including some who have left the firm, with the average per capita refund exceeding CNY1 million (USD149,745) and some in Beijing having to return as much as CNY20 million (USD3 million), amid an investigation into alleged criminal activities, according to a source familiar with the matter.

"The date for commission refund is traced back to 2019 at the earliest," the source told Yicai. The number of financial advisors required to refund commissions and the total amount are unknown yet.

On Oct. 12, the Chaoyang police in Beijing opened an investigation into CreditEase over illegal financial activities and took criminal coercive measures against the firm's executives, including actual controllers Tang Ning and Zhao Mei. Late the day before, the company sent an apology letter to its clients, admitting its quasi-fixed-income products had essentially defaulted and that it may have become insolvent after third-party institutions verified its assets.

There is a legal basis for requesting financial advisors to refund commissions obtained after CreditEase and related companies experienced a redemption crisis, Wei Bin, a partner at Beijing Long An Shenzhen Law Firm, said to Yicai. "After multiple wealth management platforms defaulted, there have been cases of notifying their ex-financial advisors to refund commissions."

First, it is necessary to distinguish the nature of commissions, Wei noted, adding that if financial products are suspected of illegal fundraising, commissions, rebates, and other earnings financial advisors obtain from selling and promoting such products may be identified as illegal income and recovered in accordance with the law. Even if financial advisors have resigned, they cannot be exempted from lawfully returning their illegal income, he stressed.

"Second, refunding commissions does not necessarily constitute a crime for financial advisors," Wei said. "In judicial practice, ordinary business personnel, organizers, and managers of illegal fundraising activities should be dealt with differently based on their subjective cognition, specific behaviors, and degree of participation. Whether financial advisors are aware of product violations, participate in false advertising, or assume management responsibilities will affect their legal responsibilities.

"But for those who knowingly and willfully engage in illegal fundraising activities to absorb public funds by means such as false advertising and promises of principal guaranteed and interest paid, as well as team leaders and managers who play an important role in illegal fundraising activities, the risk of bearing criminal liability greatly increases," he pointed out.

Some financial advisors hinted at "principal guaranteed" when recommending and selling related products, multiple investors told Yicai. According to the WeChat screenshot provided by one investor, a financial advisor said the fixed-income product the client bought was "guaranteed," meaning the product's principal and income are guaranteed.

In addition, several financial advisors used Yiren Digital (formerly Yirendai) as a credit endorsement when recommending products, including sharing news about and performance updates from the fintech firm with clients. "The underlying assets of fixed-income products are all from CreditEase's listed subsidiary Yiren Digital," one financial advisor had even said.

However, Yiren Digital has twice clarified its relationship to quasi-fixed-income products, emphasizing that, as an independent operating listed entity, it belongs to a business system independent from its parent firm's other businesses. Its operations and management are completely independent and do not affect each other, and it has not carried out any wealth management business, it added.

Established in 2006, CreditEase is one of the first financial institutions in China to provide inclusive finance and wealth management services. Its popularity grew when Yiren Digital went public in New York in 2015.

Editor: Martin Kadiev

data.title: DeepSeek Rolls Out Faster, Cheaper AI Model, Opens Search Tools to Developers
data.description:
(Yicai) Oct. 19 -- Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek has rolled out an upgraded AI model that runs faster and costs less to use, while opening its web search tools to outside developers to integrate into their own applications.

The Hangzhou-based company recently released V4.1-Flash-1017, following the debut of V4.1 Flash on Sept. 10. The update improves reasoning, coding, agent tasks, and visual performance, according to the firm, known for its low-cost options to ChatGPT and Claude.

DeepSeek described the release as a “minor update” in its technical report. The new large language model also generates shorter responses, helping users complete tasks faster and at lower cost.

DeepSeek also made its proprietary Search and Fetch interfaces, which allow developers to search the web and retrieve content from webpages, publicly available through its application programming interface. Both services cost CNY5 (75 US cents) per 1,000 calls.

The company said its search engine is designed to deliver relevant, authoritative, and timely results across multiple languages while filtering out search engine optimization spam, generative engine optimization (GEO) manipulation, and low-quality AI-generated content, aiming to provide reliable, up-to-date results.

According to DeepSeek's benchmark results, V4.1-Flash-1017 topped several tests, including the AI coding benchmark DeepSWE v1.1, the agent task completion benchmarks AutomationBench and Agents' Last Exam, and the multimodal agent benchmark Apex Bench v1.1. The model outperformed overseas competitors Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as Chinese rivals Kimi K3 and Zhipu's GLM-5.3, in those tests, according to the firm.

DeepSeek also updated DeepSeek Harness, a tool that helps AI models carry out complex tasks, to version 0.2.1 to work with the latest release. The new model was optimized for Harness during training to improve task performance while reducing runtime, output length, and token costs.

Editor: Emmi Laine
